meta.desc: How to keep your best memories, according to the data: why without cues we forget almost everything (Wagenaar’s six-year diary), from Samuel Pepys’s diary to Niépce’s first photo, how a single word changes what you remember (Loftus and Palmer), why feeling sure isn’t remembering well (Talarico and Rubin), the reminiscence bump between ages 10 and 30 (Rubin), why a smell gives you back whole years (Herz), how reliving good memories lifts your mood (Bryant), why the bad fades before the good (Walker), why telling your family’s stories builds confidence (Duke and Fivush), and a plan to keep going.

dato.wagenaar: Wagenaar publishes six years of his own diary: about 2,400 events tested with his cues
dato.pepys: Samuel Pepys starts the London diary he’ll write almost daily for nine years
dato.niepce: Nicéphore Niépce takes the oldest surviving photo: the view from his window, after hours of exposure
dato.talarico: Talarico and Rubin: 9/11 memories changed like those of any ordinary day, but confidence didn’t drop
dato.walker: Walker and colleagues: the feelings in bad memories fade faster than in good ones

recuerdoDelDia.sub: Three lines are enough: what happened, with whom and where. And a little face.
recuerdoDelDia.queEjemplo: I tried the coffee at the new stand and we laughed about the rain
recuerdoDelDia.pistas: cues: what, with whom and where
recuerdoDelDia.nota: With a single cue, Wagenaar remembered little; with what, who and where together, he recovered events he thought were lost (1986). The date was the worst cue: that’s why the card adds it on its own.

primerasVeces.listo: One a week! What’s new gets recorded: write them in your journal the same day.
primerasVeces.nota: We remember more from ages 10 to 30 because it’s the age of first times (Rubin and colleagues, 1986). What’s new gets recorded; what repeats blends into everything else.

apoyoAnecdotario.nota: A like, a subscription, or sharing it with that person you have your best memories with helps it reach more people.

grafica.pregunta: How fast were they going when they {verbo}?
grafica.vidrios: A week later: “I saw broken glass”
grafica.palabra: Same scene, a different word in the question: higher estimated speed and broken glass that was never there (Loftus and Palmer, 1974; the broken glass, in their second experiment, compared with “hit”)
grafica.joroba: What age older adults’ most vivid memories come from: the bump from 10 to 30 (Rubin and colleagues, 1986; illustrative)
grafica.masEmotivo: More emotional: it carries you away
grafica.sentidos: How emotional the memories each sense awakens are (Herz, 2004; illustrative)
grafica.revivir: A week reliving good memories for ten minutes, twice a day: happier than those who didn’t (Bryant and colleagues, 2005; illustrative)
grafica.escala: “Do you know…?”: four of the twenty questions. Tap the ones you know.

grafica.sabes2: Do you know where your grandparents grew up?
grafica.sabes3: Do you know what happened when you were born?
grafica.sabes4: Do you know what your parents’ first jobs were?
grafica.familia: Children who knew more of their family’s stories had more self-confidence and bounced back better (Duke and Fivush, “Do You Know?” scale; illustrative)
